Clinical Reference · Endocrinology

Adrenal Insufficiency & Adrenal Crisis

On this page
Failure of the adrenal cortex (primary / Addison's) or of the ACTH drive to it (secondary / tertiary) to make enough cortisol — presenting as insidious fatigue, hypotension and hyponatremia in clinic, or as fluid- and pressor-refractory shock (adrenal crisis) in the unit.
Cortisol ± aldosterone deficiency AM cortisol <3 µg/dL = deficient · >15–18 = adequate ~6–8 crises per 100 patient-yr · case-fatality ~0.5/100 pt-yr Anchor: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV — give before testing
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story

The hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis runs top-down: the hypothalamus releases CRH → the anterior pituitary releases ACTH → the adrenal cortex makes cortisol (zona fasciculata) and aldosterone (zona glomerulosa, driven mainly by the renin–angiotensin system and potassium, only weakly by ACTH). Cortisol feeds back to shut off CRH and ACTH. Adrenal insufficiency (AI) is the failure to make enough cortisol; where the break is determines what else is lost:

  • Primary (Addison's) — the adrenal gland itself is destroyed, so you lose cortisol AND aldosterone AND adrenal androgens. ACTH rises (no cortisol feedback) → the excess ACTH/POMC-derived melanocyte-stimulating peptides drive hyperpigmentation. Loss of aldosterone gives salt-wasting: hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypovolemia, metabolic acidosis.
  • Secondary — the pituitary fails to make ACTH, so only cortisol is lost. Aldosterone is intact (RAAS-driven) → no hyperkalemia, no volume collapse; ACTH is low → no hyperpigmentation. Hyponatremia still occurs, but it is euvolemic/dilutional (cortisol lack → unsuppressed ADH), SIADH-like.
  • Tertiary — the hypothalamus/CRH is suppressed, overwhelmingly by chronic exogenous glucocorticoids that a patient then stops abruptly. This is the single most common cause of AI overall.

Why cortisol matters so much: it maintains gluconeogenesis (prevents hypoglycemia), maintains vascular tone by keeping catecholamine receptors responsive (its permissive effect — without it, norepinephrine barely works, hence pressor-refractory shock), modulates immunity, and lets the kidney excrete a water load. Take it away under the stress of infection or surgery and the patient decompensates into adrenal crisis — hypotension out of proportion to any obvious cause, not fixed by fluids or pressors until steroid is given.

Cortisol is the body's on-call attending for stress. Day to day a small baseline dose keeps the lights on (glucose, blood pressure). When something big happens — sepsis, surgery, trauma — a healthy adrenal "pages back" with 5–6× the output within minutes. In AI, the attending's pager is off: baseline is thin and there is no surge. Everything looks manageable until a stressor hits, then the whole system crashes because no one answered the page. Treatment is simply putting the attending back on call — hydrocortisone replaces cortisol, and (in primary disease) fludrocortisone replaces the salt-retaining aldosterone the gland can no longer make.
HPA axis. A primary lesion destroys the gland (loses cortisol + aldosterone, ACTH rises → pigmentation); a secondary lesion cuts the ACTH drive (cortisol only, aldosterone spared by intact RAAS).
Primary vs. secondary AI — what is lost, the resulting labs, and the common endpoint: a stressor tipping into adrenal crisis.
The HPA axis with cortisol negative feedback.

The through-line for every drug in this guide: AI is a replacement problem, not a suppression problem. Hydrocortisone / prednisone / dexamethasone replace the missing cortisol (glucocorticoid) — hydrocortisone is preferred because at ≥40–50 mg/day it also covers mineralocorticoid receptors. Fludrocortisone replaces the missing aldosterone (needed only in primary disease, where the gland can't make it). DHEA optionally replaces adrenal androgens. Stress dosing mimics the cortisol surge a healthy adrenal would mount. There is no drug that "treats" AI — you give back exactly what the gland can't.

🩺 Clinic — outpatient diagnosis & lifelong replacement
Assess

When to suspect

🔍

Presentation — frequency & why it happens

AI is the great mimic: nonspecific fatigue and GI complaints for months before anyone checks a cortisol. The average patient sees several clinicians and is often mislabeled (depression, anorexia, chronic fatigue, "gastroenteritis") before diagnosis. Suspect it in anyone with unexplained hypotension + hyponatremia, weight loss + hyperpigmentation, or vasopressor-resistant shock. Frequencies below are for chronic primary AI unless noted.

Symptom / sign~FrequencyWhy it happens (mechanism)
Fatigue / weakness~100%Loss of cortisol's metabolic & permissive support; hypotension & hyponatremia compound it
Anorexia / weight loss~90%Cortisol deficiency impairs appetite/metabolism; GI dysmotility
Hyperpigmentation (skin creases, buccal mucosa, scars) — primary only~90%High ACTH/POMC → melanocyte-stimulating peptides stimulate melanocytes; absent in secondary/tertiary
Hypotension / orthostasis~55–70%Aldosterone loss (volume) + cortisol loss (↓vascular tone & catecholamine responsiveness)
GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea)~50%Cortisol deficiency; worsening GI symptoms often herald impending crisis
Hyponatremia~85–90% (primary), ~60% (secondary)Primary: aldosterone loss + volume depletion → ADH. Secondary: cortisol loss → unsuppressed ADH (SIADH-like), euvolemic
Salt craving — primary only~15–20%Renal sodium wasting from aldosterone deficiency
Hyperkalemia — primary only~35–40%Aldosterone loss → reduced renal K⁺ excretion; absent in secondary
Hypoglycemia~15–20% (higher in children & secondary)Loss of cortisol-driven gluconeogenesis; more prominent when combined GH/ACTH deficiency
Vitiligo / other autoimmune signs~10–20%Marker of polyglandular autoimmunity (APS-2)
Loss of libido / axillary–pubic hair (women)~10%Loss of adrenal androgens (DHEA) — clinically relevant only in women
Hyperpigmentation of primary AI (Addison's original 1855 plate) — creases, scars & mucosa darken from ACTH excess.

New/worsening nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and postural dizziness in a known AI patient are the classic prodrome of adrenal crisis — do not send home to "watch"; give stress-dose steroid.
Workup

What to order & when

🧪

Confirm the diagnosis, then localize the lesion

Two questions, in order: (1) Is there cortisol deficiency? — 8 AM cortisol ± cosyntropin stimulation test. (2) If yes, is it primary or central? — plasma ACTH, renin/aldosterone, 21-hydroxylase antibodies, imaging. Endocrine Society 2016 guideline.

8 AM serum cortisolFirst test in any stable outpatient. <3 µg/dL (83 nmol/L) strongly suggests AI; >15–18 µg/dL effectively excludes it; the middle is indeterminate → do a stim test.First
Cosyntropin (ACTH₁₋₂₄) stim, 250 µgConfirmatory. Measure cortisol at baseline & 30/60 min. Peak ≥18–20 µg/dL = normal (excludes AI). Gold standard for primary; may miss recent secondary (adrenals not yet atrophied).Confirm
Plasma ACTH (with the confirmatory cortisol)Localizes: high ACTH (>2× ULN) = primary; low/inappropriately normal = secondary/tertiary.Localize
Plasma renin & aldosteroneIn suspected primary AI — high renin + low aldosterone confirms mineralocorticoid deficiency (and the need for fludrocortisone).Primary
21-hydroxylase antibodiesIn confirmed primary AI — positive → autoimmune etiology (most common in high-income countries).Etiology
Electrolytes, glucose, BUN/CrEvery visit — hyponatremia ± hyperkalemia (primary), hypoglycemia.Baseline
Adrenal CT (non-contrast)In ACTH-independent (primary) AI with negative antibodies — look for TB (calcification), hemorrhage, metastases, infiltration.If Ab−
Pituitary MRIIn confirmed secondary AI — evaluate pituitary mass/apoplexy/infiltration; also screen other pituitary axes (TSH/free T4, IGF-1, gonadotropins, prolactin).If central
Very-long-chain fatty acidsYoung male, antibody-negative primary AI → screen for adrenoleukodystrophy.Selective
Adrenal CT — ordered in antibody-negative primary AI to find TB (calcification), hemorrhage, infiltration or bilateral metastases.

Interpreting the abnormal labs

LabDirection in AIMechanism & confounders / false results
8 AM cortisolLowReflects total cortisol → falsely low with low CBG (nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis, critical illness) and falsely high/normal with high CBG (estrogen/OCP, pregnancy — stop estrogen ~6 wk before testing). Prednisone/most steroids cross-react in the assay; dexamethasone does not.
Plasma ACTHHigh (primary) / Low (central)Very labile — must be spun cold and run promptly or it degrades (falsely low). Recent glucocorticoid suppresses it.
SodiumLowPrimary: aldosterone loss + volume depletion. Secondary: cortisol loss → ADH not suppressed (euvolemic, SIADH-like). Correct slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination.
PotassiumHigh (primary only)Aldosterone loss → ↓ renal K⁺ excretion. Normal K⁺ does not exclude primary AI. Hemolyzed sample can falsely raise it.
GlucoseLowLoss of cortisol-driven gluconeogenesis; worse if fasting, alcohol, or concurrent GH deficiency.
ReninHigh (primary)Volume depletion + aldosterone loss activate RAAS; confirms mineralocorticoid deficiency.
TSHMildly highCortisol normally restrains TSH; can mimic hypothyroidism and normalizes after steroid replacement — don't chase it until cortisol is replaced.
Eosinophils / calciumHighCortisol normally suppresses eosinophils; mild eosinophilia & occasional hypercalcemia are classic supportive clues.

Cosyntropin (250 µg) Stimulation Test — interpreter

Enter the peak cortisol (baseline, 30 or 60 min — use the highest). Threshold per Endocrine Society 2016 (assay-dependent; newer monoclonal assays may use ~14–15 µg/dL).

Treat

Chronic replacement

💊

Lifelong replacement — glucocorticoid, mineralocorticoid, androgen

You are replacing the two hormones the axis can no longer supply. Glucocorticoid (hydrocortisone) is universal; mineralocorticoid (fludrocortisone) is added only in primary disease, because in secondary/tertiary AI the RAAS-driven aldosterone system is intact. Dose to the lowest amount that relieves symptoms without Cushingoid excess — there is no blood test that titrates glucocorticoid replacement, so it is clinical.
1
Glucocorticoid replacement — the anchor (all AI)
Hydrocortisone is first-line; longer-acting agents for adherence
▾
DrugStartTitrationTarget / MaxWhy / when to pickIf intolerant / alt
Hydrocortisone (default)15–25 mg/day PO in 2–3 divided doses, largest on waking (e.g. 10 mg wake / 5 mg early afternoon, or 10/5/5)Adjust by 2.5–5 mg per dose q2–4 wk to symptoms~15–25 mg/day total (children ~8 mg/m²/day); avoid dosing after ~6 PM (insomnia)Short-acting → mimics diurnal cortisol; ≥40–50 mg/day also covers mineralocorticoid receptorsPrednisolone if HC unavailable
Prednisolone / prednisone3–5 mg PO once daily (morning)±1 mg q2–4 wk3–5 mg/dayOnce-daily → better adherence; longer half-life smooths troughsUse prednisolone (active) in liver disease
Dexamethasone0.25–0.75 mg PO nightly±0.25 mg0.5 mg/day typicalVery long-acting; no assay cross-reactivity (useful when cortisol must be measured)Hard to titrate; Cushingoid risk — not preferred
Modified-release hydrocortisone (Plenadren; Chronocort/Efmody)Convert total daily HC dose, once (Plenadren AM) or twice (Chronocort) dailyPer product conversionPhysiologic diurnal profileRestores overnight/early-morning cortisol rise; may improve QoL & metabolic markersCost/availability limited
Unknown home dose? Restart at a standard physiologic dose — hydrocortisone 15–20 mg/day (e.g. 10 mg AM + 5 mg midday) — and titrate clinically. When sick and unable to confirm, err on the side of stress dosing.

Side effects / monitoring: over-replacement → weight gain, central adiposity, hypertension, hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, insomnia; under-replacement → fatigue, nausea, hypotension, crisis. Monitor weight, BP, glucose, symptoms — not serum cortisol or ACTH for titration.

2
Mineralocorticoid replacement — primary AI only
Fludrocortisone; titrate to renin, BP, K⁺
▾
DrugStartTitrationTarget / MaxWhy it worksIf intolerant / alt
Fludrocortisone50–100 µg PO once daily (morning)±50 µg q1–2 wk to targets50–200 µg/day (rarely up to 300)Potent mineralocorticoid → restores Na retention & K⁺ excretion the failed gland can'tLiberalize dietary salt; high HC doses give some mineralocorticoid effect
Titrate fludrocortisone to: normal supine/standing BP without orthostasis, normal Na⁺/K⁺, and plasma renin in the upper-normal range (high renin = under-replaced; suppressed renin + hypertension/edema = over-replaced). Do not add fludrocortisone in secondary/tertiary AI — aldosterone is intact.

Monitoring: supine & standing BP, electrolytes, edema; renin at follow-up. Excess → hypertension, hypokalemia, edema; deficit → salt craving, orthostasis, hyperkalemia.

DHEA (optional) + the rules that prevent crisis

Sick-day rules (the single most important patient education)

SituationGlucocorticoid action
Fever <38 °C / minor illnessDouble usual oral hydrocortisone until recovered
Fever ≥38 °C / infection needing antibioticsTriple usual oral dose (or up to 3×)
Vomiting / diarrhea / can't keep pills downIM hydrocortisone 100 mg (emergency kit) & seek care — do not rely on oral
Minor surgery / dental / colonoscopyExtra 25–50 mg HC on the day; resume normal dosing next day
Moderate surgeryHC 50 mg IV at induction → 25 mg q8h × 24 h, then taper over 1–2 days
Major surgery / trauma / laborHC 100 mg IV then 50 mg q6h (or 200 mg/24 h infusion); taper over 2–3 days
Every AI patient needs a hydrocortisone 100 mg IM emergency injection kit, a steroid emergency card, MedicAlert identification, and trained family — this is a Society for Endocrinology / Endocrine Society standard, not optional.

Prevent

Prevention, USPSTF & comorbidities

🛡️

Keeping AI patients out of crisis

There is no USPSTF screening recommendation for adrenal insufficiency itself (it is not a screenable general-population condition). The relevant Grade A/B recommendations apply to the consequences and comorbidities of lifelong steroid replacement:

GradeRecommendationRelevance to AI
BOsteoporosis screening (DXA)Chronic glucocorticoid raises fracture risk — screen & treat
BScreen for abnormal glucose / prediabetes (BMI ≥25, age 35–70)Glucocorticoid over-replacement worsens glycemia
BDepression screening (adults)Under-/over-replacement and DHEA deficiency affect mood; commonly missed pre-diagnosis
A/BBlood pressure screeningFludrocortisone dosing depends on it

Vaccinations: AI patients are functionally at higher infection-related crisis risk — keep influenza (annual), COVID-19, and pneumococcal (PCV20 or PCV15→PPSV23) up to date. Physiologic replacement is not immunosuppressive, so live vaccines are generally permitted at replacement doses (individualize).

Comorbidity interactions

ComorbidityEffect on AI courseManagement change
Hypothyroidism (autoimmune, APS-2)Thyroid hormone ↑ cortisol clearance — starting levothyroxine first can precipitate crisisReplace cortisol before thyroid hormone; may need to increase HC when thyroxine started
Type 1 diabetesLoss of cortisol's counter-regulation → more hypoglycemia; sick days destabilize bothSick-day rules for both; watch glucose during stress dosing
PregnancyRising CBG & placental CRH; cortisol needs rise in 3rd trimester↑ HC ~20–40% in 3rd trimester; stress-dose in labor (HC 100 mg then q6h); fludrocortisone may need ↑ (titrate to BP/K, not renin — renin normally rises)
Other autoimmune (APS-1/APS-2: vitiligo, pernicious anemia, celiac, premature ovarian insufficiency)Cluster with primary AI; celiac can impair oral absorptionScreen periodically; treat celiac to restore steroid absorption
CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, St John's wort)Accelerate hydrocortisone metabolism → under-replacement/crisisIncrease glucocorticoid dose (often 2×) while on the inducer; monitor closely
CYP3A4 inhibitors / estrogen (OCP, ritonavir, itraconazole)Estrogen ↑ CBG (may need more HC); inhibitors ↑ steroid levelsAdjust dose; interpret cortisol assays with caution
Drugs to avoid / use with caution: Etomidate (blocks 11β-hydroxylase — can precipitate crisis; use ketamine for RSI if possible). Abrupt steroid withdrawal of any kind. Starting levothyroxine before glucocorticoid. Rifampin/phenytoin/carbamazepine without a compensatory HC increase. Ketoconazole, mitotane, checkpoint inhibitors impair cortisol synthesis/gland. Diuretics can worsen hyponatremia/orthostasis.
Escalate

When to refer / admit

🚑

Red flags → ED / admission

Send to ED / admit for: hypotension (SBP <100) or orthostasis with symptoms, persistent vomiting/diarrhea (can't take oral steroid), Na <125 or K >6.0, hypoglycemia, fever/sepsis in a known AI patient, altered mentation, or any suspected adrenal crisis.
If crisis is suspected, give hydrocortisone 100 mg IM/IV in clinic before transfer — do not wait for labs or the ED. Under-treatment kills; a dose of hydrocortisone in a patient who turns out not to have AI is harmless.
Refer to endocrinology for: new diagnosis, difficult titration, planned pregnancy/surgery, suspected pituitary disease (needs MRI + full anterior-pituitary workup), or recurrent crises.
🛏️ Wards — acute inpatient stabilization
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria & initial profile

  • Suspected or confirmed adrenal crisis or hemodynamic instability (SBP <100, orthostasis with symptoms).
  • Symptomatic or severe hyponatremia (Na ≤125, or ≤130 with symptoms), significant hyperkalemia, or hypoglycemia.
  • Intractable vomiting/diarrhea preventing oral steroid replacement.
  • Newly diagnosed AI needing IV stabilization, education, and titration.
  • Intercurrent illness (sepsis, MI, surgery, trauma) in a known AI patient requiring parenteral stress dosing.
The bar for admitting a known-AI patient with any acute illness is low — the same illness a well person shrugs off can tip an AI patient into crisis within hours. When in doubt, admit and stress-dose.

Treat

Acute management

💊

Stepwise inpatient therapy

1
Steroid + volume + glucose
The three simultaneous priorities
▾
InterventionStartTitrationTargetWhy it works
Hydrocortisone IV100 mg IV bolusthen 50 mg IV q6h or 200 mg/24h continuous infusion200 mg/24h until stableReplaces cortisol; restores vascular tone & catecholamine responsiveness; ≥200 mg/24h intrinsically covers mineralocorticoid needs
0.9% saline1 L over first hourguided by volume/hemodynamics~4–6 L in first 24h (individualize)Corrects the aldosterone-loss volume deficit; raises Na⁺ toward normal
DextroseD50 bolus for acute hypoglycemiaD5-containing maintenance fluidGlucose >70 mg/dLReplaces cortisol-dependent gluconeogenesis
2
Treat the precipitant
Crisis rarely happens without a trigger
▾

Culture and treat infection (most common), and look for MI, trauma, surgery, missed doses, new CYP3A4 inducer, or recent levothyroxine start. Fixing the trigger is as important as the steroid.

3
Taper & reintroduce fludrocortisone
As the patient stabilizes (24–72h)
▾

Once hemodynamically stable and the precipitant is controlled, taper hydrocortisone by ~50%/day toward oral maintenance (15–25 mg/day divided). In primary AI, reintroduce fludrocortisone 50–100 µg once total HC falls below ~50 mg/24h — above that, hydrocortisone's own mineralocorticoid activity is sufficient.

Convert to oral only when the patient is tolerating PO, hemodynamically stable, and the precipitant is resolving. Give a written sick-day plan before any downgrade toward discharge.

Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Escalation triggers

Transfer to ICU for: persistent/worsening shock despite fluids + stress-dose steroid (needs vasopressors), hyperkalemia with ECG changes, severe symptomatic hyponatremia needing controlled/monitored correction, refractory hypoglycemia, airway or consciousness compromise, or severe underlying sepsis/organ failure.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: hemodynamically stable; tolerating oral glucocorticoid at maintenance dose; electrolytes & glucose normalizing; precipitant treated; and — non-negotiable — the patient leaves with an emergency injection kit, steroid card, MedicAlert, written sick-day rules, and confirmed endocrine follow-up.

Crisis prevention is the single most effective intervention. Do not discharge a new-diagnosis AI patient without hydrocortisone injection training for patient + caregiver and a filled fludrocortisone prescription (primary AI).

Home

Stable, educated, self-manages oral + injectable steroid; has kit & follow-up.

Home health

Needs nursing reinforcement of injection technique / med reconciliation at home.

SNF

Deconditioned or unable to self-administer; needs 24h skilled nursing for steroid management.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Prolonged crisis/critical illness with deconditioning; can tolerate ≥3h therapy/day.

LTAC

Complex prolonged recovery (e.g., post-ICU vent weaning after crisis-related sepsis).

Hospice / palliative

AI from advanced malignancy (adrenal metastases) with comfort-focused goals.
🫀 ICU — adrenal crisis & refractory shock
Admit

ICU triggers

🚨

When it belongs in the unit

Adrenal crisis is the ICU face of this disease: life-threatening hypotension/shock that is refractory to fluids and vasopressors but responsive to glucocorticoid. Escalate to ICU for vasopressor-requiring shock, hyperkalemia with ECG changes, severe symptomatic hyponatremia needing monitored correction, refractory hypoglycemia, or altered consciousness/airway compromise.

The defining move is hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately — before labs, before imaging, before the stim test. Under-treatment is lethal; an unnecessary dose is harmless.
Allolio crisis criteriaMajor health impairment plus ≥2 of: hypotension (SBP <100), nausea/vomiting, severe fatigue, fever, somnolence, hyponatremia (≤132) or hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia — plus improvement after parenteral glucocorticoid.
Adrenal crisis algorithm — steroid + volume + glucose simultaneously, then pressors only if shock persists (Society for Endocrinology / Endocrine Society 2016).
Treat

Crisis protocol & CIRCI

⛑️

Dose ladder — hydrocortisone, fluids, glucose

InterventionStartTitrationTarget / MaxWhy it works
Hydrocortisone IV100 mg IV/IM push STATthen 50 mg IV q6h or 200 mg/24h continuous infusion (sickest: 100 mg q6h)200 mg/24h; taper ~50%/day once stableRestores cortisol → vascular tone & catecholamine responsiveness (the permissive effect); high dose also covers mineralocorticoid receptors
0.9% saline1 L in the first hour (up to ~1000 mL/h in profound shock)guided by hemodynamics/CVP/lactate~4–6 L in first 24hReverses aldosterone-loss hypovolemia; corrects hyponatremia
DextroseD50 IV bolus if hypoglycemicD5-containing infusionGlucose >70Replaces cortisol-dependent gluconeogenesis
Dexamethasone (only if diagnosis unconfirmed)4 mg IVreplace with HC once stim test donebridge onlyCovers the patient without corrupting the cortisol assay
At stress-dose hydrocortisone (≥200 mg/24h) no fludrocortisone is needed — its mineralocorticoid effect is intrinsic. Reintroduce fludrocortisone (primary AI) only when HC tapers below ~50 mg/day.

CIRCI — critical-illness-related corticosteroid insufficiency (SCCM/ESICM 2017)

Distinct from primary/secondary AI: critical illness (esp. septic shock, ARDS) can produce functionally inadequate cortisol activity. Diagnosis: delta cortisol <9 µg/dL after 250 µg cosyntropin, or random cortisol <10 µg/dL (both imperfect). Treatment: IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day (50 mg q6h or infusion) for vasopressor-dependent septic shock; the guideline suggests against steroids in sepsis without shock. In early moderate–severe ARDS, methylprednisolone ~1 mg/kg/day.

Support

Pressors & access

💉

Which drip, why, and the dose

Access & monitoring: arterial line for beat-to-beat BP, central line if on vasopressors, hourly urine output, Na⁺/K⁺/glucose q2–4h during active correction, continuous telemetry.

AgentReceptors / mechanismDose rangeHemodynamic effectWhen to pick
Norepinephrineα1 ≫ β10.01–0.5+ mcg/kg/min↑SVR, mild ↑CO, little tachycardiaFirst-line once fluids + steroid insufficient
VasopressinV1 (catecholamine-independent vasoconstriction)Fixed 0.03 units/min↑SVR; norepinephrine-sparingAdd-on when α-receptors down-regulated / to spare catecholamines
Epinephrineβ1/β2 + α10.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑CO + ↑SVR (↑lactate, ↑HR)Third-line / refractory
In true adrenal crisis, catecholamine pressors are relatively ineffective until glucocorticoid is given — cortisol is permissive for α1-receptor expression and post-receptor signaling. Steroid is the definitive "pressor" here; norepinephrine is a bridge to MAP ≥65 while the hydrocortisone takes effect.
Correct

Electrolytes — with cautions

🧫

Hyponatremia & hyperkalemia

Hyponatremia — correct SLOWLY. Giving cortisol/fludrocortisone + isotonic saline switches off ADH → a brisk free-water diuresis and a fast Na⁺ rise. Limit to ≤8–10 mmol/L in 24h (≤6–8 if chronic/high-risk); check Na⁺ q2–4h; be ready to give free water ± DDAVP to re-lower if overshooting — this is a classic setting for osmotic demyelination.

Hyperkalemia (primary AI): IV calcium (membrane stabilization) if ECG changes; insulin+glucose and β-agonist to shift; but hydrocortisone + volume + resolving acidosis usually correct K⁺ on their own. Avoid K-sparing agents, ACEi/ARB, NSAIDs.

Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Downgrade when: off vasopressors and hemodynamically stable on stress-dose steroid; hypoglycemia resolved; electrolytes correcting at a safe rate (Na rise ≤8–10/24h); precipitant controlled; and tolerating enteral intake with the steroid taper under way.

Not yet if: still requiring any vasopressor, Na⁺ moving faster than target (needs q2–4h monitoring), ongoing uncontrolled sepsis, or unable to take oral steroid. Before floor transfer, ensure the oral regimen, fludrocortisone reintroduction plan (primary AI), and patient education are documented.

Evidence

Pearls & landmark trials

💡

12 practice-changing pearls

  1. Never delay hydrocortisone for a stim test. In suspected crisis, treat first; if you must preserve diagnostics, use dexamethasone 4 mg IV (no cortisol-assay cross-reactivity) and test later.
  2. Stress-dose hydrocortisone (≥200 mg/24h) covers mineralocorticoid needs — fludrocortisone is unnecessary during crisis; only restart it (primary AI) once HC falls below ~50 mg/day.
  3. Secondary/tertiary AI does NOT need fludrocortisone — aldosterone is RAAS-driven and intact.
  4. Hyperpigmentation is a clue to PRIMARY AI only (ACTH/POMC excess); its absence never excludes AI.
  5. Treat cortisol BEFORE thyroid hormone. Levothyroxine first accelerates cortisol clearance and can precipitate crisis.
  6. Vomiting/diarrhea = inject, don't swallow — GI illness defeats oral absorption; go straight to IM/SC hydrocortisone 100 mg.
  7. Hyperkalemia + hyponatremia together → think primary AI; isolated euvolemic hyponatremia can be secondary AI masquerading as SIADH.
  8. Correct hyponatremia slowly (≤8–10 mmol/L/24h) — steroid + saline switches off ADH → brisk aquaresis → overcorrection & osmotic demyelination risk.
  9. Etomidate can cause AI after a single dose (11β-hydroxylase inhibition) — consider ketamine for RSI in these patients.
  10. Immune checkpoint inhibitors cause AI — both hypophysitis (secondary) and primary adrenalitis; low threshold to test oncology patients with fatigue/hypotension.
  11. CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, St John's wort) accelerate hydrocortisone clearance — increase the glucocorticoid dose to avoid under-replacement.
  12. Glucocorticoid-induced (tertiary) AI is the commonest cause overall — anyone on >5 mg prednisone-equivalent/day for >3–4 weeks may have HPA suppression; taper slowly and stress-cover.
🧪

Landmark trials

TrialYearResultWhy it matters
Annane2002 (JAMA)HC 50 mg q6h + fludrocortisone 50 µg × 7d ↓ 28-day mortality in cosyntropin non-respondersLaunched low-dose steroid + mineralocorticoid in septic shock; introduced stim-test stratification
CORTICUS2008 (NEJM)No mortality benefit; faster shock reversal; stim test did NOT predict response; more superinfectionTempered enthusiasm; abandoned routine stim-test stratification
ADRENAL2018 (NEJM)Continuous HC 200 mg/d × 7d: no change in 90-day mortality (27.9% vs 28.8%); faster shock resolution & extubationLargest trial — HC hastens recovery but doesn't reduce mortality
APROCCHSS2018 (NEJM)HC 50 mg q6h + fludrocortisone: ↓ 90-day mortality 43.0% vs 49.1% (NNT ≈17)Positive mortality signal; revived interest in adding fludrocortisone in sicker cohorts
Endocrine Society cosyntropin validation2016250 µg cosyntropin peak cortisol ≥500 nmol/L (18 µg/dL) excludes AIDiagnostic gold standard for AI
ADRENAL (neutral) vs APROCCHSS (positive) diverge on the addition of fludrocortisone, bolus dosing, and a sicker cohort — the "hydrocortisone ± fludrocortisone in septic shock" debate remains open, with 2024 analyses leaning toward adding fludrocortisone.
